Article Title: Ancy Sojan: Thrissur girl who broke 22-year-old record, now aiming for Asiad gold
Article Text:
Kerala's Ancy Sojan (PTI Photo)

Forged in sand

Backwater bounty

Kerala vs Karnataka: Record rivalry

Kerala vs Karnataka

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: Ancy Sojan was around three when Anju Bobby George launched herself into the air at the end of a brisk run-up in Athens and set a seemingly unsurpassable national long-jump record. For much of the two decades that followed, Ancy may not have spent a lot of time thinking about George’s record, because her sights were set elsewhere, on the athletics track — remarkable for someone who would eventually overhaul the mark that had stood for 22 years.Now, the girl from Thrissur in central Kerala is looking to write the next chapter in the story at next month’s Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. She’ll get to warm up for Japan at two events in India. The first of those comes next week in Bhubaneswar, the city where she jumped 6.88m in June to better George’s 6.83m set in 2004.Gearing up for another stab at international glory — she had won the long-jump silver at the last Asian Games — if the 25-year-old gets a moment to reflect on her journey, she would undoubtedly find herself back on the vast shoreline of Nattika, the unlikely setting that put her on the path to becoming an elite athlete.Ancy’s father, an autorickshaw driver, used to bring his daughter to the beach in Nattika, where she would sprint on the loose sands, dreaming of becoming a sprinter. But destiny had other plans.“Unknowingly, Ancy was putting herself through nature’s own strength training programme. Running on that loose sand builds strength in the calves and ankles,” said P Ramachandran, the sprinter from Nattika who competed in the 2000 Sydney Olympics 4x400m relay.Ancy’s coach, Anoop Joseph, echoes the thought.“Running on the uneven surface of the sand forces your ankles, feet and core to stabilise your body. It can help maintain control during approach and takeoff,” he explains.Ancy made the switch to long jump around 2015, when she won bronze with a 4.93m jump at the U-14 state school games. Then, in 2019, she burst onto the Indian athletics scene with a 6.26m jump at the National School Athletics meet in Sangrur, Punjab.Sanoj VV, her childhood coach who played a pivotal role in Ancy’s transition from a sprinter to a long jumper, remembers the spark he had seen then.“Back then I had predicted that Ancy would break George’s national record. People laughed at me. Today my prediction has come true,” he said, adding that “it was remarkable considering she was so tiny back then”.Following her feat in Bhubaneswar, accolades have poured in for Ancy from several quarters, including a congratulatory call from Kerala chief minister V D Satheeshan.When asked about his ward’s 6.88m leap, Anoop, however, chose to downplay it.“Technically, it was a perfect jump. But let’s not get carried away. We’re still working on her motor qualities, speed and strength,” he said.Anoop has a point. Records in women’s long jump tend to have surprising longevity. The world record, of 7.52m, was set by erstwhile USSR’s Galina Chistyakova in 1988, the same year that the US’ Jackie Joyner-Kersee set the Olympic record of 7.4m at Seoul.Ancy had won her Asian Games silver with a jump of 6.63m, much below her best. The gold in the last edition, held in China, was bagged by the host country’s Xiong Shiqi with a 6.73m jump.For Ancy, the run-up to Japan — apart from the World Athletics Continental Tour in Bhubaneswar, which begins on August 22, she’ll also take part in the Indian Athletics Series in Delhi from September 10 — comes against the backdrop of a personal worry.“My father is recovering from an injury, and his mobility remains restricted. He has not resumed driving his autorickshaw. It remains a concern,” she told TOI.A fishing hamlet known for its frequent dolphin sightings, Nattika is also part of cinema lore as the backdrop for the timeless, National Award-winning Malayalam film ‘Chemmeen’. Part of its claim to fame is also the raft of Olympians and international athletes that it has given India.Apart from Ramachandran, Nattika has produced Anjali P D, a track athlete, and discus thrower Athulya P. Volleyball also has a good following in this sports-loving village.“But no one from Nattika has managed to capture the national imagination like Ancy,” Ramachandran said.Yet, the village lacks a Sports Authority of India centre and is still waiting for a 400m synthetic track for budding athletes.“Aspiring athletes from Nattika have to travel to Kunnamkulam or the SAI centre in Palakkad, which typically takes at least two hours of travel by road,” Ramachandran said.In recent years, Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha has been campaigning for a synthetic track at the Corporation Stadium in Thrissur.“The progress has been slow,” said Sanoj VV.Sanoj had trained his ward till she was 18 at a ramshackle sand pit on the fringes of the National Fisheries Higher Secondary School in Nattika.“We created a makeshift sand pit for Ancy’s training back then,” he said. “Last year, the government inaugurated a modest 200-metre synthetic track here.”The progression of the national women’s long-jump record has been a two-way battle between Karnataka and Kerala. The elite list features no more than seven athletes who’ve held the record since Karnataka’s Angel Mary Joseph became the first Indian to breach the 6m mark in 1978.Till Ancy Sojan set the new mark of 6.88m in Bhubaneswar in June this year, the honours were evenly split between the two southern states.Mercy Mathew, who held the record in the early 1980s, says she was surprised that Anju Bobby George’s stay at the top lasted 22 years.Talking about Ancy, she feels the girl from Thrissur is capable of bigger leaps.“I wonder why it took this long (for George’s record to be broken), though there were quite a few who looked capable of breaking her mark,” she said. “Those were the days when we knew nothing about records. My first national record came at the inter-university meet in February 1980 in Pune,” she recalled.Mercy said Ancy is capable of adding another 10-12cm to the new record.“I’ve seen her progress from the days when she competed at the school games. She is an aggressive athlete and is capable of giving her best under pressure,” Mercy, who runs her own athletics academy in Kochi, told TOI.Mercy’s best of 6.26m came at the 1982 Asian Games, where she won silver.George’s era began with a record-breaking 6.37m on August 3, 1999, and she then took charge of the record book, improving her mark before producing her personal best of 6.83m in the 2004 Olympics final.
Article Summary: Ancy Sojan won the long-jump silver at the last Asian Games. She jumped 6.88m in June to better Anju Bobby George’s 6.83m set in 2004. The 25-year-old is looking to write the next chapter in the story at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games next month.

Article Title: How VVS Laxman & Co. kept Manav Suthar on India’s radar
Article Text:
India's Manav Suthar (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jaipur: When Manav Suthar went unsold at the IPL auction ahead of the 2023 season, disappointment was natural. The left-arm spinner had put together a stellar domestic run, taking 39 wickets in six Ranji Trophy matches in 2022-23, and hoped a franchise contract would provide another platform to showcase his craft.But there were enough signs to tell him that his efforts were not going unnoticed.That year brought a Duleep Trophy call-up and a place in the India A squad for the ACC Men’s Emerging Teams Asia Cup, where he finished with 10 wickets in five matches.Fast-forward to the present and the 24-year-old from Rajasthan is the talk of the town after spinning India to a dominant 165-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first Test in Galle. Suthar finished with 10 wickets in the match — four in the first innings and six in the second — to underline why he has long been considered one of the most exciting left-arm spin prospects in the country. The years spent grinding away on the domestic circuit have undeniably begun to pay off.Suthar’s journey towards the senior India side had, in fact, begun much earlier. His first significant exposure to the national set-up came in February 2019, when he made his India Under-19 debut in the first ‘Youth Test’ against South Africa Under-19 in Thiruvananthapuram.With Rahul Dravid then overseeing the youth programme, Suthar returned four wickets in the match, including 3/44 in the second innings, as India won by nine wickets.It was in such environments that his ability to extract bite from the surface while retaining control began to attract attention. When VVS Laxman took over as head of the National Cricket Academy in 2021, Suthar’s progress continued to be closely tracked.According to his long-time coach in Sri Ganganagar, Dheeraj Sharma, Laxman’s interest went beyond merely keeping an eye on the numbers.Sharma recalled how Laxman had alerted then chief selector Chetan Sharma.“Laxman had told Chetan Sharma that ‘he is a very good spinner, do watch him’. So he came specially to watch,” Dheeraj said.That visit could hardly have been better timed. When Chetan travelled to Jodhpur to watch Suthar in Rajasthan’s Ranji Trophy match against Chhattisgarh in January 2023, the youngster produced the kind of all-round performance that makes a selector take notice.He remained unbeaten on 64 in Rajasthan’s first innings before claiming 10 wickets in the match.For a young left-arm orthodox spinner coming through at a time when India have naturally begun considering their options for the years beyond Ravindra Jadeja, Suthar’s skill set has made him particularly intriguing.Dheeraj, who has worked with him since his early days, had long impressed upon his ward that his greatest strength lay in being different.“I always used to tell him that his skill set is not present in any other left-arm orthodox spinner. That skill is now part of his muscle memory,” he said.
Article Summary: Manav Suthar went unsold at the IPL auction ahead of the 2023 season. The 24-year-old from Rajasthan is the talk of the town after spinning India to a dominant 165-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first Test in Galle.

Article Title: 195-run lead! Joe Root's England leave Pakistan on the ropes at Headingley after day 2
Article Text:
England's Joe Root bats on day two of the first Test match between England and Pakistan in Leeds, England, Thursday Aug. 20, 2026. (AP)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

England took control of the first Test against Pakistan on Thursday, finishing Day 2 on 366/8 and taking a first-innings lead of 195 runs at Headingley.Joe Root, Harry Brook, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence all scored half-centuries after England resumed from 112/2. Rain delayed the start of play by nearly four hours, but England's batters made the most of the time available.Harry Brook, the world's No. 1 Test batter, came closest to a century. Playing on his home ground, he scored 91 before left-arm spinner Ali Usman bowled him. Brook hit 13 fours during his innings. Usman finished with 5/92, the first five-wicket haul of his Test career.Brook had an early escape after being dropped on one by stand-in Pakistan captain Salman Agha at second slip. He made Pakistan pay before being dismissed with nine runs left for a hundred.Root and Cox added 150 runs for the third wicket after play resumed. Cox scored 73 in just his second Test, while Root made 66.Cox reached his first Test fifty before Root brought up the 109th fifty of his Test career. Root, who has scored more than 14,000 Test runs, was later trapped lbw by Khurram Shahzad after missing a straight delivery. He reviewed the decision, but replays showed the ball was hitting middle stump.Cox also missed out on a bigger score. He was dropped on 57 by Khurram Shahzad in a caught-and-bowled chance before edging Ali Usman behind.Dan Lawrence, playing his first Test in two years, added 51 runs in the middle order. England scored at 4.46 runs per over.Pakistan's bowling and fielding struggled for long periods after the visitors were dismissed for 171 on the opening day.At stumps, wicketkeeper Jamie Smith was unbeaten on 16, while Jofra Archer was yet to score. England will begin Day 3 with a 195-run lead and two wickets in hand.
Article Summary: England finish Day 2 on 366/8 and take a first-innings lead of 195 runs at Headingley. Joe Root, Harry Brook, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence all scored half- centuries. Rain delayed the start of play by nearly four hours.

Article Title: BFI reopens Asiad selection, Sumit Kundu loses 70kg spot to Deepak Punia
Article Text:
India's Kapil Pokhariya, in red, competes (PTI Photo)

TOI

New Delhi: In a surprise move that has raised questions over the finality of India’s Asian Games boxing selection, the Boxing Federation of India (BFI) conducted fresh trials at NIS Patiala on Aug 17, weeks after announcing its squad for the Aichi-Nagoya Games.has exclusively learnt that the federation held one-off selection bouts in three categories — men’s 70kg and 90kg, and women’s 65kg — pitting the boxers originally selected for the Asiad against their respective reserves.The move comes despite the BFI’s May 13-15 selection trials at NIS, where the squad for both the Glasgow Commonwealth Games and Asiad was finalised. It was understood then that the team would remain unchanged, and the selected boxers subsequently travelled to the CWG.However, following recommendations from the high-performance unit, support staff and selection committee, the BFI reopened the three categories. The biggest casualty was 70kg boxer Sumit Kundu, who had been part of the announced Asiad squad. Sumit lost his bout to reserve Deepak Punia and was consequently relegated to reserve, with Punia taking the Games berth.The minutes of the Aug 17 trials, accessed by TOI, state: “The boxer who wins the selection trials and secures Rank 1 in the trial shall be selected to represent the country at the Asian Games 2026.”They further specify that the Rank 2 boxer would be retained as reserve.The minutes, however, carried a caveat: “If the sports ministry and IOA do not accept the revised entries, the boxers who represented India at the CWG in these categories will retain their Asian Games places.”In the other two categories, the original selections survived. Kapil Pokhariya beat reserve Harsh Choudhary in the 90kg bout, while Parveen Hooda defeated Saneh in the women’s 65kg category.BFI sources said the fresh assessment was necessitated after the three boxers failed to win medals at the CWG. Sumit lost in the pre-quarters, while Kapil and Parveen bowed out in the quarters. Sources added the federation's view was to maximise India’s medal prospects by sending the best boxers.Sumit is expected to travel as a reserve for the pre-Games training camp, though a recent injury means he may focus on recovery. He is also considering a move to men's 80kg to avoid repeated weight cuts, with next year’s Olympic qualification cycle in mind.
Article Summary: Boxing Federation of India conducted fresh trials at NIS Patiala on Aug 17. Move comes weeks after announcing its squad for the Aichi-Nagoya Games. Boxing federation held one-off selection bouts in three categories. The biggest casualty was 70kg boxer Sumit Kundu, who had been part of the announced Asiad squad.

Article Title: Delhi’s invisible opponent: How drift is becoming a factor at the World Championships
Article Text:
New Delhi: USA's Garret Tan being attended by a physio after an injury (PTI Photo)

New Delhi:

Box Items:

WHAT'S DRIFT?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

H

OW DRIFT CHANGES THE GAME

In a sport decided by precision and where the smallest margins can separate a winner from a loser, the most talked-about variable at the Indira Gandhi (IG) indoor stadium is something players cannot see. It is the air.At the BWF World Championships , the much-discussed “drift” has emerged as an additional tactical challenge, compelling shuttlers to recalibrate their strokes, movement and shot selection almost from rally to rally. With air-conditioning and ventilation creating differing currents across the arena, the four courts are not playing alike — and even the two ends of the same court can demand different solutions.The effect is most pronounced on Centre Court 1 and adjacent Court 3, where airflow from the AC vents creates noticeable side drift. Court 2 has also shown some movement, though comparatively less troublesome, while Court 4, farther from the strongest vents, has remained largely stable.For players, that difference can be decisive. Lakshya Sen experienced it immediately in his opening-round victory over Austria’s Collins Valentine Filimon. The Indian struggled to find his range early, particularly with delicate net play, before shrinking his stroke production and bringing Filimon into longer exchanges."I adapted after the change of ends, opened up the rallies and stopped playing the short, flat exchanges that had initially allowed him (Filimon) to dictate," Sen had said after his win. The conditions, however, were not the sole reason for Sen's defeat to American Garret Tan on Wednesday.Kodai Naraoka’s assessment was even more revealing. In his three-game victory over Chi Yu Jen, the Japanese shuttler found one half markedly quicker while the opposite side appeared to hold the shuttle back. The contrast was stark enough to contribute to a 21-12, 7-21, 21-16 scoreline. "The side opposite to the audience was the fast one. On the other hand, the shuttle was not travelling for me. It was sometimes stopping before I could reach the net," Naraoka said.Ayush Shetty’s headline-making upset of world No. 1 and defending champion Shi Yu Qi was also a case in point. Shetty prevailed 21-14, 13-21, 21-19, but the Chinese star repeatedly appeared uncomfortable when playing from the more difficult end on the Centre Court, particularly while lifting the shuttle.Coach Vimal Kumar felt the drift affected Shi’s judgement and timing, especially when he had to send the shuttle high and deep. "The challenge in drifty conditions is that once the shuttle is in the air, it can float unpredictably, making it difficult to make the perfect connection when attacking, especially on the smash," he explained.Canadian Victor Lai described the shuttle as unusually floaty and said players had to shorten their swings, sharpen their strokes and be wary of cross-court shots being carried beyond the lines. "...Got used to the conditions a bit better. One side there’s drift: one side is slower and one side’s faster. The side drift’s not crazy strong, but still a little bit. The wind blows the shuttle very strong. But honestly, I have kind of gotten used to it a lot of places like this, China, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand too, a lot of these Asian countries have this sort of drift. I won’t say like I am perfect, but I am getting used to it," he told BWF media.The drift has also been part of the backdrop to Indian losses on Court 3, including men's doubles pair M R Arjun and H Amsakarunan’s defeat to South Korea’s M H Kang and D Ki. Unnati Hooda, who pushed Michelle Li to 23-21 in the decider, also saw crucial side pushes drift beyond the lines."It was for both (the drift). We have to adjust to conditions as players. I thought of switching to flick serves but then didn't do it," Unnati said.While badminton remains a game of skill, nerve, execution and tactics, but in Delhi, players are discovering that mastering the air is equally important.Drift is the sideways or directional movement of air inside an indoor badminton hall. Unlike outdoor wind, it is generated by ventilation, air-conditioning, temperature differences, humidity, doors opening and closing, and even crowd movement.When the shuttle enters a moving air current, its trajectory can change subtly but significantly.A shuttle travelling with the airflow can move faster or carry deeper; against it, the same stroke may slow, dip or fall short. Cross-drift can push flat shots and lifts sideways. Players therefore alter racket speed, swing length, smash power, lift height and positioning. The result is a constant process of recalibration — especially when changing ends, where the same shot may require a completely different touch.
Article Summary: Air-conditioning and ventilation create differing currents across the arena. Effect is most pronounced on Centre Court 1 and adjacent Court 3. Court 4, farther from the strongest vents, has remained largely stable. Lakshya Sen experienced it immediately in his opening-round victory.

Article Title: Lakshya Sen suffers stunning upset, but Ayush Shetty and PV Sindhu march on
Article Text:
India's PV Sindhu (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Delhi: A stunned silence swept across the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium as India’s premier men’s singles hope, Lakshya Sen, cracked under the weight of expectations. In a major upset at the BWF World Championships 2026, the world No. 14 shuttler crashed out in the second round, humbled 19-21, 21-19, 21-17 by USA’s unheralded Garret Tan, ranked 92nd, in a gruelling 73-minute contest.Lakshya’s display on Wednesday was alarmingly inconsistent, plagued by baffling errors in judgement. While Tan grappled with the drift, Lakshya appeared perpetually unsettled.Much like his sluggish opening-round encounter, Lakshya started at a pedestrian pace, searching fruitlessly for timing while the American settled quickly. The Indian did manage to summon a fleeting burst of resolve midway through the opening game, rattling off late points to erase a deficit, level the score and snatch the opener 21-19.Yet, any expectations that the opening-game heist would settle Lakshya’s nerves were swiftly extinguished.The ensuing two games exposed glaring tactical vulnerabilities. Missing routine shots proved to be Lakshya’s bane. Even as he scrapped to stay within touching distance in the second game, Tan held firm in the clutch moments to edge it 21-19 and draw level.The decider laid bare Lakshya’s unravelling. A barrage of unforced errors leaked from his racquet. The contest took a dramatic turn when Tan began suffering from severe cramps midway through the third game.Writhing in pain between points, it momentarily seemed the American might be forced to retire. Yet, rather than pouncing on a physically compromised opponent, Lakshya remained hesitant and flat-footed. Showing remarkable courage, Tan soldiered through to keep his nose in front.Though Lakshya attempted a frantic late fightback, the gap was simply too wide to bridge.“I would give a lot of credit to my opponent; he played a very solid game. I think I gave it my all in the end, but it was just not enough to win this match,” Lakshya said.While Lakshya’s shock exit cast a shadow over the home crowd, the 21-year-old sensation Ayush Shetty provided an electric lift. Shetty dismantled Sri Lanka’s Duminda Abeywickrama 21-8, 21-10 in a breathless 26-minute masterclass to cruise into the pre-quarterfinals.Two-time Olympic medallist PV Sindhu also advanced to the pre-quarters, subduing Canada’s Wen Yu Zhang 21-16, 21-17 in 35 minutes. Although Zhang staged a brief fightback to draw level in the second game, Sindhu shifted gears midway to pull away for a straight-games victory.However, there was heartbreak for 18-year-old Unnati Hooda in the women’s singles draw. The teenager pushed Canada’s experienced 13th seed Michelle Li to the absolute limit across 58 minutes before narrowly bowing out 21-11, 9-21, 21-23.India’s mixed doubles pairing of Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto raced past Macau’s Leong Iok Chong and Ng Weng Chi 21-11, 21-11 in just 30 minutes to advance.The men’s doubles campaign suffered a setback as Arjun MR and Hariharan Amsakarunan lost 17-21, 14-21 to South Korea’s Kang Min Hyuk and Ki Dong Ju in 43 minutes.Satwik-Chirag duo gets walkoverIndia’s top-ranked men’s doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty moved into the pre-quarterfinals without hitting a shot after Scotland’s Alexander Dunn and Adam Pringle withdrew from their scheduled second-round clash here on Wednesday.
Article Summary: Lakshya Sen, India's premier men's singles hope, cracked under the weight of expectations. The world No. 14 shuttler crashed out in the second round, humbled by USA’s unheralded Garret Tan, ranked 92nd, in a gruelling 73-minute contest.

Sourav Ganguly's shirt-waving celebration at Lord's in 2002 has been recreated 24 years later, this time by India's Mixed Disability cricket team.After India defeated England by 118 runs in a T20 match at Lord's on August 19, India's players took off their shirts and waved them in the air, recalling Ganguly's famous celebration after India's NatWest Trophy final win over England at the same venue in 2002.The celebration came after India put up 206 for four, their highest score of the seven-match series. England were then bowled out for 88 as India completed a 118-run win at the Festival of Disability Cricket.The victory, however, came after England had already secured the series 4-3.India's batting effort was shared among several players, with Arjun Gaware, Major Magray and Sai Akash among those who contributed with the bat.England's bowlers struggled to contain India's scoring. Alfie Pyle took two wickets, but the visitors' total proved too much for England to chase.England needed a strong response to record their first win at Lord's, but their innings ended at 88.England captain Callum Flynn said: “It’s such a disappointing end for us, we’ve fought so hard this series and done so much right and I felt it was all leading to a sign-off win here, but it wasn’t to be."While England took the seven-match series 4-3, their wait for a win at Lord's continues after India's victory at the venue."Hopefully in a year’s time we’ll get a chance to get our first win at Lord’s. As cricketers with disabilities, some of us might have imagined we’d never get the chance to play here - the next step now is getting a win here," Flynn said.The mixed-disability format combines players from varied impairments, including physical, hearing, and learning problems.
Article Summary: India defeated England by 118 runs in a T20 match at Lord's on August 19. Players took off their shirts and waved them in the air, recalling Ganguly's famous celebration after India's NatWest Trophy final win over England at the same venue in 2002.

Article Title: Ace jockey Suraj Narredu ready for Japan test
Article Text:
Suraj Narredu

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Having booted home more than 2,400 winners and won every premier race in India, Bengaluru-based jockey Suraj Narredu has been seeking international challenges in recent years. After competing in the prestigious Shergar Cup at Ascot Racecourse in the UK for two consecutive years, the 41-year-old, who hails from a family of jockeys and trainers, is set for another international experience this weekend.Suraj will compete in the World All-Star Jockeys (WASJ) competition hosted by the Japan Racing Association (JRA) at Sapporo Racecourse in Hokkaido. He will be the first Indian jockey to ride in the annual event, which features six international riders. Besides Suraj, the international contingent includes jockeys from South Africa, Australia, France and Canada. They will take on Japanese riders in the four-leg competition, with two races scheduled on Saturday and two on Sunday.“It is a big honour to be a part of the event, especially since I’m the lone Asian to be invited. It's a competition between Japan's jockeys and the rest of the world,” Suraj told TOI.The event is significant not just for the prize money — the winning jockey takes home $19,300 — but also because a JRA license is at stake.“If you can finish individually in the first five placings in the points, then you are eligible to get a short-term license in Japan for the following year. The short-term license is a three-month license, which is otherwise very difficult to obtain,” explained Suraj.“I’m looking at the bigger picture. I want to perform well so that I get a chance to ride in Japan on a short-term license. It’s one of the world's best racing jurisdictions,” he added.Having established himself as one of the country's leading jockeys, Suraj believes his search for international opportunities is also driven by the changing landscape of Indian horse racing.“The racing scene in India is not exactly as smooth as it used to be. I have probably reached a stage where I’ve won every big race that has to be won in India. In 2023, when I competed in Australia, that’s when I felt very stagnated in terms of my performance because I was winning races here.Still, I was never elevating myself to ride better or work harder,” Suraj said.After his recent stint in the UK and with the Japan challenge ahead, Suraj says the international exposure has given him fresh motivation to push himself further.“I changed my entire routine recently because at the international events I wanted to be the best version of myself,” he signed off.
Article Summary: Suraj Narredu will compete in the World All-Star Jockeys (WASJ) at Sapporo Racecourse in Hokkaido. He will be the first Indian jockey to ride in the annual event, which features six international riders. Besides Suraj, the international contingent includes jockeys from South Africa, Australia, France and Canada.

Article Title: The Sanju Samson void and search for Kerala’s next T20 star
Article Text:

Fan groups from across the world are calling for FIFA president Gianni Infantino to step down after his controversial attempt to sell future World Cup profits to private investors.The petition, launched on Thursday with the hashtag #InfantinoOut, also demands major changes to FIFA to prevent similar controversies in the future.The petition was backed by groups including Football Supporters Europe, Football Supporters Africa and North America’s Independent Supporters Council, along with around 40 national fan organisations.“The shameful attempt by one individual — the FIFA President himself — to sell off the World Cup to private investors exposed a betrayal football will never forget,” the petition said, referring to Infantino’s proposed commercial spin-off, which he abandoned after strong opposition.The groups argue that Infantino has lost the trust of football supporters. UEFA has said it has no confidence in him, while officials from CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation have also criticised his leadership.“Gianni Infantino has demonstrated a profound failure of leadership, incompatible with democratic governance,” the fan petition states. “The concentration of power around the FIFA Presidency, combined with opaque decision-making, personality cult clientelism, and zero accountability has destroyed any remaining trust in the world governing body."“For the credibility of FIFA — and for the future of the game — he must resign,” the petition adds.The supporters also point to Infantino’s earlier controversial positions, including his backing of the proposed European Super League and his push for the World Cup to be held every two years.The fan groups say these decisions have further damaged trust in FIFA and strengthened their demand for a change in leadership.

Article Title: Sam Curran ruled out for rest of English season with groin injury, Test comeback delayed
Article Text:

England all-rounder Sam Curran has been ruled out for the remainder of the English season after being advised to undergo surgery on a groin injury, ending his hopes of making a Test comeback this summer.Curran, 28, will undergo an operation on Friday and will miss Surrey’s remaining matches as well as England’s white-ball series against Sri Lanka in September. The injury is a major setback for the all-rounder, who had emerged as a potential option for England’s Test side following Ben Stokes’ retirement.Curran last played Test cricket in 2021 but had been under consideration for a recall during England’s ongoing series against Pakistan. Selector Marcus North had suggested Curran could have been in contention for the first Test had he not been managing his fitness during The Hundred.North had also indicated that Curran could potentially come into consideration for the third Test, scheduled to begin on September 9. Further assessment of the groin problem, however, has now ruled out that possibility.Curran’s fitness concerns had already affected his involvement in The Hundred.The Surrey all-rounder missed one match for MI London and did not bowl his full allocation in four of their other seven group games.He had also pulled out of this year’s Indian Premier League in March because of a groin issue.Curran’s absence further complicates England’s balance as they look to rebuild their Test combination following Stokes’ retirement. Without Curran, Stokes or another seam-bowling all-rounder, England opted against selecting a frontline spinner for the first Test against Pakistan at Headingley.Instead, Dan Lawrence was promoted to No. 6 and asked to contribute with his part-time off-spin as England sought a different way to balance the side.Another Surrey all-rounder, Will Jacks, is also currently sidelined after undergoing an operation to remove his appendix. Jacks, who performed a similar role during last winter’s Ashes, was left out of Surrey’s squad for Thursday’s County Championship match against Nottinghamshire.The ECB said Jacks’ recovery would be monitored before his availability for England’s T20 and ODI series against Sri Lanka is assessed.“Neither Sam Curran nor Will Jacks are in Surrey’s squad for today’s resumption of the Rothesay County Championship. Sam Curran has been assessed for a groin injury and will undergo surgery on Friday. He will not be available for the remainder of the home season,” the ECB said in an injury update.“Will Jacks is currently recovering having had a successful operation to remove his appendix. We will monitor his recovery and assess availability ahead of the Sri Lanka series.”

Article Title: ‘The landscape is very different now’: Joe Root explains captaincy comeback, opens up on McCullum exit and Fleming era
Article Text:
Joe Root (Reuters Photo)

Four years changed Root’s perspective

Root ‘gutted’ by McCullum exit, backs Fleming

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Joe Root could hardly have asked for a better start to his return as England Test captain, but his comeback is less about reclaiming an old role and more about embracing a challenge he now feels better equipped to handle.Root had previously described his relationship with the England captaincy as unhealthy before stepping down. Four years on, however, he believes his circumstances, experience and perspective have changed significantly.“Well, first and foremost, I think the landscape is very different now. You look back at that time, we were just sort of coming out the other side of COVID, and as a team we'd spent 20-odd games in those kind of environments,” Root told Sky Sports.“And if I'm being brutally honest, I think having to do that for so long, it wasn't really the in-game stuff that wore me down. It was the stuff that surrounded it, and being involved in things that weren't what you'd normally expect to be involved in as an England captain.”Root said the prolonged circumstances eventually affected both his enjoyment of the role and his ability to get the best out of himself and his players.“I think they sort of bled into everything else, and it got to a point where I wasn't enjoying it anymore, I wasn't getting the best out myself, certainly wasn't getting the best out of the players,” he said.“But I also think that was a byproduct of having to live the way that we were living for such a long period of time. You marry that up with playing India twice and Australia as well within that period, it makes things very difficult, and it got to the point where it was time for someone else to take over.”Root believes the time away from captaincy has given him a different understanding of the game and left him uniquely prepared for another stint as leader.“And the last four years have been probably four of the most enjoyable of my career. I got to see the game slightly differently, look at it through a different lens, which, as you know, once you've captained, you do look at the game slightly differently afterwards,” he said.“And I feel in a really unique position now where I have that experience. Not many people get the chance to do it again. And the world is a very different place. I've four years more experience, a lot more games under my belt, worked with Brendan and Baz in a slightly different capacity, and feel really readied for the challenge that lies ahead.”Asked why he was confident the captaincy would not affect him in the same way again, Root offered a light-hearted response.“Yeah, I mean, unless we find ourselves in another pandemic. No, I think things are very different now, and how I manage my way through that will be very different as well.”Root also admitted he was disappointed by Brendan McCullum’s departure as Test coach, having credited him with bringing out the best in his cricket.“Yeah. I mean, I'll be honest with you, I was gutted when I found out Brendan was no longer going to be the Test coach. He's someone that I feel has really got the best out of me personally,” Root said.“I've loved the way he sees the game and the way that he's opened my eyes up to looking at it slightly differently, even after 120-odd games or whatever it was by the time he took over.”Root said he was pleased McCullum would continue with England’s white-ball teams and added: “someone that I owe a huge amount to. I've become pretty close with over that period of time as well.”At the same time, Root expressed excitement about working with new Test coach Stephen Fleming, whom he has admired since his playing days.“We've crossed paths a bit over the last few years when he's coached different teams around the world, but someone I've always admired,” Root said.He praised Fleming’s experience, calmness and record in high-pressure environments, adding that the new coach “creates a brilliant environment for the lads to thrive in.”
Article Summary: Joe Root has returned as England Test captain after four years out of the role. Root says he feels better equipped to handle the role than he did four years ago. Root admits he was 'gutted' by Brendan McCullum's departure as Test coach.

The ICC has removed the demerit point given to Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium pitch after the third ODI between Pakistan and Australia in June.The decision comes after the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) and Cricket Canada appealed against demerit points awarded for matches played that month.The ICC Appeals Panel reviewed video footage, match referee reports and comments from the captains before overturning the original decision."The demerit point imposed on Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium, following an 'Unsatisfactory' rating for the third Men’s ODI between Pakistan and Australia on 4 June, has been rescinded. The panel noted that while the guidelines of the ICC Pitch and Outfield Monitoring Process were followed by the Match Referee, 'the pitch did not demonstrate excessive unevenness or spin'," said ICC in a statement.The panel said the pitch used on June 8 was in line with the standard expected from a satisfactory surface.It also found that the wicket “did not demonstrate excessive unevenness, seam movement or spin”, leading to the demerit point being withdrawn.Pakistan had won the three-match ODI series against Australia 2-1. Despite the pitch controversy, spin played a major role throughout the series, with spinners from both teams making an impact in all three matches.

Article Title: England pacers cut Pakistan Test match ball in half after first innings; here's why
Article Text:
Josh Tongue and Ollie Robinson

England pacers Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared the wickets and later shared the match ball after both finished with five-wicket hauls on the first day of the first Test against Pakistan at Headingley on Wednesday.Robinson took 5 for 51 and Tongue claimed 5 for 46 as Pakistan were bowled out for 171 on the first day of England's first Test under Joe Root's second stint as full-time captain following Ben Stokes' retirement from international cricket.England ended the day on 112 for 2, with Root unbeaten on 37, trailing Pakistan by 59 runs.Robinson gave England the perfect start by taking a wicket with the first ball of the match. He went on to remove four Pakistan top-order batters before Tongue completed the innings with the remaining wickets.Since both bowlers took five wickets, they decided to split the match ball instead of one player keeping it as a souvenir. A member of the Headingley ground staff cut the ball into two halves for them.Showing one half of the ball during his post-match press conference, Robinson explained how the idea came about."As we were walking off Tonguey said, 'I think we should split it'. I was like, 'yeah, we should actually do that, I think it'd be quite cool'.""I said 'do you reckon they'll be able to do it?' and within five minutes they brought it back up and it was done.""It’s one of those things that you don't really have too many halves of….half a cricket ball. It's something we'll never forget really and it's not too often two guys get five in the same innings, so it’s a nice gesture and something to remember."Earlier this summer, Robinson took a career-best seven wickets in an innings against New Zealand, his first Test appearance in more than two-and-a-half years.The 32-year-old then missed the second Test against New Zealand because of a knee injury and was not selected for the third Test at Trent Bridge despite being available."It was frustrating not to be able to play at the Oval, it was just a bit of a freak training injury and then I was available for Trent Bridge but not selected.""I was ready to go but I suppose that's part of professional sport, isn't it? I've just worked really hard on a bit more fitness and a bit more skill, so it's nice when it comes off on days like today."
Article Summary: England pacers Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared the wickets and later shared the match ball after both finished with five-wicket hauls. Robinson took 5 for 51 and Tongue claimed 5 for 46 as Pakistan were bowled out for 171 on the first day of England's first Test against Pakistan.

Article Title: 'I practised with Kookaburra ball at home': Manav Suthar's grind behind Galle heroics

Manav Suthar

India left-arm spinner Manav Suthar said practising with the Kookaburra ball before the Sri Lanka series helped him adapt quickly to the conditions as he played a key role in India's win in the first Test in Galle.Suthar picked up 10 wickets in only his second Test as India defeated Sri Lanka by 165 runs on Wednesday to take a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.The 22-year-old took 6 for 55 in Sri Lanka's second innings and finished with match figures of 10 for 101, helping India wrap up the victory on the fifth day.Speaking in a video released by the BCCI, Suthar said he had started preparing with the Kookaburra ball after India's match against Afghanistan and spent plenty of time practising with it before leaving for Sri Lanka."I take Test cricket very seriously. My focus is to improve day to day when I go to practice. I practice as much as I can. My focus after the Afghanistan game was to adapt as soon as possible. I practised a lot with the Kookaburra ball. I practised in nets and at home."Suthar also said India's decision to arrive in Sri Lanka 10 days before the Test gave him enough time to understand the conditions and get used to bowling with the Kookaburra ball."We came to Sri Lanka ten days ago, and it helped a lot in adapting to the environment and how to play with the Kookaburra ball. I get time to adapt. It has helped me a lot."The spinner said patience was important on the Galle pitch and revealed that he discussed the approach with Ravindra Jadeja and Kuldeep Yadav during the match."We were talking about how patiently we can play. We knew that it would be difficult for the new batsmen to play on this wicket."Suthar said India's victory meant more to him than his personal performance.“The most important thing is that we won the match. That is the most important thing. I am very happy about that. I am very happy that I was able to perform in the team’s victory. Winning is the best thing.”He added that beginning the series with a win has given India momentum heading into the second Test.“It is very important because you get momentum when you start this series. You get a good rhythm. You get momentum as a team. It helps a lot. Everyone feels good when we win. I would like to say that it is very good. Winning is the best thing.”Suthar will now look to carry his form into the second Test against Sri Lanka, which begins on August 23.

The journey

The last time Qamran Iqbal played competitive cricket, it took him nearly 2,800 kms and a frantic 15 hours to get there. Called up at short notice, the 24-year-old endured a chaotic journey that has stayed with him ever since. This time, though, there is no last-minute scramble. Iqbal arrived at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence (CoE) four days before the Duleep Trophy, giving himself time to settle in and prepare for the challenge ahead.Iqbal is one of six members of Jammu & Kashmir’s Ranji Trophy-winning side picked for North Zone, and they will open their campaign against West Zone from Sunday. "My last Bengaluru trip was something else," Iqbal tells TimesofIndia.com.Six months ago, on February 23, a day before the Ranji Trophy final, Qamran Iqbal was relaxing at his home in Srinagar when, around 3 pm, his phone rang. Jammu and Kashmir needed him in Hubballi, nearly 2,800 kms away, after opener Shubham Khajuria was ruled out with an injury.The 24-year-old immediately embarked on a cross-country journey, arriving at the venue barely an hour before the toss. Less than 24 hours after receiving the call-up, Qamran produced the innings of his life, scoring an unbeaten 160 in the second innings to steer Jammu and Kashmir to their maiden Ranji Trophy title, defeating Karnataka on the basis of the first-innings lead."Everything happened suddenly," he says."I left Srinagar that same night. I took a late-night flight and travelled through Delhi and Mumbai before reaching Hubballi. I arrived around 8 in the morning on match day and went almost straight to the ground. A day earlier, I was somewhere else and suddenly I was playing a Ranji Trophy final. It felt a little strange."I wasn't feeling pressure as such, but there was some travel fatigue. Still, it was fine because everyone in the team contributed. It was truly a team effort, and that's why we won. It was a dream come true for the entire team. Winning the Ranji Trophy was a special feeling for everyone associated with Jammu and Kashmir cricket. It felt really good," he continues.The youngster, who once opened the batting alongside Yashasvi Jaiswal for India Under-19, cherishes the Ranji Trophy triumph but insists it is only the beginning. Having been named in North Zone's 15-member Duleep Trophy squad, he is determined to achieve bigger things."I want to achieve a lot more in my cricket career. Winning the Ranji Trophy for the first time made me very proud, and I was happy that I could contribute to the team's success. But this is only the beginning. I want to achieve much more," he says.Earlier this year, Aqib Nabi, in an exclusive interview with TimesofIndia.com, spoke about how the arrival of P. Krishnakumar as bowling coach helped transform his bowling. Qamran also credits the Jammu and Kashmir Cricket Association management, particularly current BCCI president Mithun Manhas , for creating a roadmap that eventually led to the historic Ranji Trophy triumph."For the last two or three years, the entire support staff and management have backed us completely. The association regularly sends us on exposure tours. Mithun sir has been working with us for the last four or five years and has created an excellent structure during the off-season. He regularly visits our camps, and we play tournaments like the Buchi Babu Tournament and other invitational competitions before the domestic season. It has made a huge difference," says Qamran."Mithun sir has played a massive role in developing cricket in Jammu and Kashmir. Because of the exposure he has given players during the off-season, it becomes much easier to perform once the domestic season begins. Ajay Sharma sir, our coach, has also been outstanding. He has played cricket at the highest level, and the small technical tips he gives us are extremely valuable."Qamran started as an U-14 in Jammu and Kashmir cricket. He believes the standard of the sport and infrastructure has improved tremendously in the past few years."Since Mithun sir came in, the facilities have improved a lot. We now have different types of wickets to prepare on, including turf wickets, grass wickets and spin-friendly surfaces. The overall infrastructure has become much better, and players now have access to everything they need."Before every domestic season, we play tournaments like the Buchi Babu Tournament against strong teams from other states. Those matches build confidence. When you step into domestic cricket, you don't feel like it's your first game because you've already played quality cricket during the pre-season. That experience has helped me immensely," he says.Qamran's father, Dr. Iqbal, is a doctor by profession and a passionate cricket follower. It was he who encouraged his son to pursue the sport."My father took me to the ground for the first time. He wasn't a cricketer himself, but he loved the game and was very interested in cricket. He introduced me to the sport when I was playing Under-14 cricket at the Sher-e-Kashmir Cricket Stadium," he recalls."From there, I progressed through the age groups. I played Under-16, then Under-19, represented North Zone and eventually made it to the India Under-19 setup."Qamran narrowly missed out on India's squad for the 2020 Under-19 World Cup, but he still treasures his time with the national junior side, where he opened the batting alongside Yashasvi Jaiswal."I was part of that group and played three series with the India Under-19 team. I wasn't selected for the World Cup squad, but being in that environment was a great learning experience. I performed reasonably well in India Under-19 cricket. I had several scores in the 80s and 90s, but I couldn't convert them into a century. I think that made the difference, and I missed out," he says.
Article Summary: Qamran Iqbal scored an unbeaten 160 in the second innings of the Ranji Trophy final against Karnataka. The 24-year-old travelled nearly 2,800 kms from Srinagar to Hubballi to play in the final. He was called up to the Jammu & Kashmir side after opener Shubham Khajuria was ruled out with an injury. Qamran has been named in the North Zone squad for the Duleep Trophy.

Article Title: ‘Don’t go chasing the IPL’: Cheteshwar Pujara’s plea for Manav Suthar after Galle heroics
Article Text:
India's Manav Suthar (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manav Suthar’s impressive start to his Test career has already sparked comparisons with Ravindra Jadeja , but former India batter Cheteshwar Pujara believes the young left-arm spinner should prioritise his red-ball development rather than chasing an Indian Premier League contract.Suthar has played only two Tests for India but has already made a significant impact. The 24-year-old followed up his five-wicket haul on debut against Afghanistan in New Chandigarh earlier this year with a match-winning 10-wicket performance in Galle.Suthar claimed six wickets in Sri Lanka’s second innings as India completed a 165-run victory in the first Test to take a 1-0 lead in the series.With the youngster showing strong potential in the longest format, Pujara urged both Suthar and the Indian management to protect his development as a red-ball specialist.“Try to preserve him. We have had this discussion in the past that, yes, all the young players might want to play the shorter format, but India should be looking to preserve him for the Test format. Yes, he might want to play the IPL, but don't go there. I mean, yes, if he gets the opportunity to play the IPL, that's fine, but don't change your strength,” Pujara said on the Sony Sports Network.Pujara does not believe Suthar needs to make major changes to his bowling to succeed in white-ball cricket.He said the spinner can play in the IPL if the opportunity comes his way, but cautioned him against altering the qualities that have made him effective in Tests.“I think he doesn't need to change his bowling much. Just when it comes to white-ball cricket, you need to have that flatter trajectory, and I don't mind him playing in the IPL. If he plays in the IPL, if he's successful in the IPL, that is fine, but don't change your strength,” he added.Suthar is currently contracted with Shubman Gill’s Gujarat Titans in the IPL. However, his exposure in the tournament has been limited. He has played only five matches and taken two wickets, with four of those appearances coming during the 2026 season and one in the 2024 edition.Pujara believes Suthar’s natural ability to bowl slowly and flight the ball is precisely what makes him such an exciting prospect in Test cricket.“For someone like Manav Suthar, who is flighting the ball, who is willing to go a little slower, when it comes to red-ball cricket, you don't need to change that. Don't change yourself just for the IPL. I can understand, but don't change your natural ability, which is to flight the ball," said Pujara.The former India No. 3 also pointed to Suthar’s willingness to attack with flight even when the ball was new as one of the reasons behind his success against Sri Lanka.“When you look at his bowling in the first innings and even while the ball was new, he was willing to flight the ball, put the ball in the right areas. The way he has bowled, I think India has found a proper left-arm spinner who will be there in the squad for a long time,” he added.Suthar’s breakthrough performance in Galle came at an important time for India. The Test was wrapped up during the second session on the fifth and final day, with rain forecast for the remainder of the day. Suthar and Ravindra Jadeja ensured India completed the job without having to worry about a weather intervention.The victory gave India valuable World Test Championship points and put them 1-0 ahead in the two-match series.India will now look to complete a series whitewash when they face Sri Lanka in the second Test, beginning in Colombo on August 23.
Article Summary: Manav Suthar has made an impressive start to his Test career. Cheteshwar Pujara believes the young spinner should prioritise red-ball development rather than chasing an Indian Premier League contract. The 24-year-old claimed six wickets in Sri Lanka’s second innings as India completed a 165-run victory in the first Test.

Article Title: Spain break 23-year-old international cricket record held by Ricky Ponting and Steve Waugh's Australia
Article Text:
Spain cricket team (left) and Ricky Ponting

How Australia's record was set

Not Australia, England, India or Pakistan. Spain have become the team with the longest winning streak in international cricket, breaking the record previously held by Ricky Ponting and Steve Waugh's Australia.Spain are currently playing in the Men's T20 World Cup Sub Regional Europe Qualifiers in Southern Finland and have won all their matches in the tournament so far. Their latest victory came against Bulgaria on August 18, when they chased down a target of 60 in just 29 deliveries, winning by nine wickets.Spain moved past Australia's record when they beat Finland in their opening match on August 14. That victory was their 21st in a row in international cricket, taking them one win beyond Australia's previous record of 20.They have since extended the streak to 24 consecutive victories after beating the Isle of Man, Luxembourg and Bulgaria.Spain's 24-match winning run has included T20I series against the Isle of Man and Jersey, as well as two series against Croatia. The two Croatia series were separated by the ICC Men's T20 World Cup Sub Regional Europe Qualifier in 2024, where Spain finished second after one of their matches was abandoned.Australia's previous record of 20 consecutive international wins came across Tests and ODIs under Waugh and Ponting.The run began on January 11, 2003, when Australia beat England in Hobart. It continued until the third Test against the West Indies in Bridgetown in May 2003.Australia's winning run finally ended when the Waugh-led side lost the fourth Test against the West Indies.During that period, Australia went unbeaten in the 2003 ODI World Cup after winning all their matches in a tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka. They then switched to Test cricket and won three matches against the West Indies.Ponting captained Australia in the ODI tri-series and the World Cup, while Waugh led the team in Tests.Australia played 17 ODIs and three Tests during their 20-match winning streak.Spain have now gone past that mark, extending their international winning run to 24 matches.
Article Summary: Spain break Australia's record of 20 consecutive international wins. Ricky Ponting and Steve Waugh's side won 17 ODIs and three Tests in 2003. Spain are currently playing in the Men's T20 World Cup Sub Regional Europe Qualifiers in Southern Finland.

Article Title: 'Virat Kohli was better than Sachin Tendulkar in Tests': AB de Villiers makes huge claim

Sachin Tendulkar and Virat Kohli (Agency Image)

AB de Villiers believes Virat Kohli took India’s batting success in overseas Test cricket to another level, while crediting Sachin Tendulkar for first showing that Indian batters could thrive in conditions traditionally considered difficult for players from the subcontinent.The former South Africa batter and Kohli’s ex-Royal Challengers Bengaluru teammate was speaking after India’s 165-run victory over Sri Lanka in Galle on Wednesday.De Villiers acknowledged Tendulkar’s pioneering role but argued that Kohli went a step further in establishing himself as an outstanding overseas Test batter.“I think of someone like Sachin Tendulkar way back, who started that trend for India. Yet, he wasn’t as strong as someone like Virat Kohli, who was even better. But Sachin was the first guy to show that as a subcontinent batter, you can do well in bouncy and seaming conditions. Virat took that forward and raised the bar,” said de Villiers on his YouTube channel.Tendulkar remains the highest run-scorer in Test cricket, having accumulated 15,921 runs in 200 matches before retiring in 2013. Kohli, who retired from Test cricket in May 2025, ended his career with 9,230 runs in 123 Tests, placing him 19th on the all-time list.The statistics, however, suggest Tendulkar still holds the edge when it comes to performances away from home. Of his 15,921 Test runs, 8,705 came outside India, accounting for around 55% of his total. He is also the leading run-scorer among batters in overseas Test cricket.Kohli scored 4,774 runs in 66 Tests outside India.The comparison remains in Tendulkar’s favour even when the focus is restricted to SENA countries: South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia. Tendulkar amassed 5,387 runs in 63 Tests in those countries at an average of 51.30, including 17 centuries and 23 fifties.Kohli, meanwhile, scored 3,661 runs in 46 Tests in SENA conditions at an average of 42.08, with 12 centuries and 14 fifties.De Villiers’ assessment therefore appears to focus less on the raw numbers and more on Kohli’s wider influence on Indian Test cricket. During Kohli’s tenure, India established itself as a formidable side overseas, setting higher expectations for performances outside home conditions.According to de Villiers, that influence has carried into the current generation, with batters such as KL Rahul and Devdutt Padikkal following the path laid by Tendulkar and Kohli.“Because of that, there are quite a few players now like [KL] Rahul and [Devdutt] Padikkal, who have started to up that trend and follow in the footsteps of a Virat and a Sachin,” he added.De Villiers did, however, identify overseas batting as an area where Rahul needs to improve. Despite praising the Karnataka batter’s technique and importance to the Indian side, he pointed out that Rahul averages only 34 away from home.“KL is a guy with a sound technique and is a big asset in that Indian lineup. But he averages only 34 away from home. So you’ll expect more and that is one area where he has to work on. He has to get bigger scores once he gets in and not just get a 100 but make it a 180 because that first-ball duck and getting out to the newish ball is always around the corner. So for him, the name of the game will be to make the big scores even bigger,” said de Villiers.De Villiers’ comments come as India look to build on their Galle victory and continue developing a new generation of batters capable of maintaining the country’s strong record in challenging overseas conditions.
Article Summary: AB de Villiers believes Virat Kohli took India’s batting success in overseas Test cricket to another level. The former South Africa batter credited Sachin Tendulkar for first showing that Indian batters could thrive in conditions traditionally considered difficult for players from the subcontinent. Kohli ended his career with 9,230 runs in 123 Tests, placing him 19th on the all-time list.

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest.
